title: Market Signals From The Yen And US Bonds
gist: Gavekal's Anatole Kaletsky argues that summer 2026 produced three simultaneous cases of 'market madness': AI-equity speculation, an irrationally cheap yen, and bond investors' misplaced faith that the Fed will return inflation to 2%. He rates the latter two mispricings as more important than the widely-discussed AI bubble.

themes.theme: Mispricing as the source of alpha

insights.claim: The adage that 'the market is always right' is close to exactly wrong: most securities are correctly priced most of the time, but at any moment some assets are being completely mispriced, and finding those is the core trading opportunity.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Frames portfolio effort around hunting a small number of egregious mispricings and waiting for realignment, rather than broad market timing.
insights.quote: the cliché that “the market is always right” is almost exactly wrong
insights.locator: When it comes to financial markets

insights.claim: Three distinct mispricings escalated into 'market madness' during summer 2026: speculation in AI-related equities, an extremely cheap yen, and bond investors' faith in a return to 2% US inflation.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Three concurrent dislocations imply a menu of convergence trades: short AI froth, long yen, and short the bond market's inflation complacency.
insights.quote: three cases of mispricing escalated into what I called “market madness”
insights.locator: This summer, three cases of mispricing

insights.claim: The cheapness of the yen and the bond market's inflation complacency are arguably more important mispricings than the widely-discussed AI equity bubble, which is described as the obvious one that everybody has discussed.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Consensus attention is concentrated on AI valuations; the less-crowded risk-reward may sit in FX and rates, where positioning is more one-sided against the author's view.
insights.quote: the two other mispricings are arguably even more important: the crazy cheapness of the yen; and the irrational faith among bond investors that the Fed will return inflation to its 2% target.
insights.locator: The obvious one, which everybody has discussed

insights.claim: Bond investors' expectation that the Federal Reserve will bring inflation back to its 2% target is characterized as irrational faith, implying US yields are too low and inflation risk is underpriced.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Argues for underweight duration and long inflation-protection exposure if the 2% anchor fails to hold.
insights.locator: the irrational faith among bond investors
